newsitem.title: INDIA: India government safe for now, key ally says.
newsitem.headline: India government safe for now, key ally says.

text.p: India's Congress party said on Wednesday that it will not immediately move to topple the United Front government it has reluctantly supported for nine months.

"It won't fall this year," Congress spokesman Vithal Gadgil told Reuters when asked if Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's government might fall during the three-month long budget session of parliament which opens on Thursday.
"It will at least survive the budget session," Gadgil said.

Deve Gowda has fewer than 200 deputies in the 545-member lower house of parliament. The Congress, which controls some 140 deputies, said over the weekend its support for the government was no longer unconditional.

The Congress Working Committee, the party's main policy-making body, issued a statement accusing the United Front minority coalition of failing to work with it to fight against the Hindu nationalist opposition.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram is scheduled to unveil the nation's budget for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) on February 28.

Gadgil's remarks were the strongest indication so far that the Congress, which suffered its worst-ever defeat in last year's general elections, was not about to precipitate the mid-term election that would follow if Deve Gowda were to lose his majority.

India's oldest political machine, Congress is reeling from a string of financial scandals dogging its leading politicians, and suffered a humiliating defeat earlier this month in the northern farming state of Punjab.

Congress's pledge to keep Deve Gowda's government going seemed to have little effect on the rightwing Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which has said it is considering moving a no-confidence motion against the United Front.

"The shadow of uncertainty is looming large on this government's chances of survival," said Krishan Lal Sharma, vice president of the BJP, which is the largest single group in parliament's lower house.

Sharma said the BJP was weighing the no-confidence motion in the hope of widening a rift between the Congress and the United Front over a host of economic issues and a 1986 artillery deal known as the "Bofors scandal".

The federal investigating agency this month revealed the names of five people who it said had received payments from Sweden's Bofors AB in the $1.3 billion howitzer deal. It said more names could be revealed later.
Bofors said last week it saw no need to reopen the investigation into the contract, and added that the firm had paid money as final payments to its agents, not as bribes.

Congress politicians say the scandal has been deliberately revived by Deve Gowda to embarrass their party. Congress lost the 1989 general elections over the Bofors issue after then prime minister Rajiv Gandhi was accused of involvement in the affair.
Gandhi, who denied the allegations, was assassinated while campaigning for 1991 parliamentary polls.
"There could be a lot of smoke from the Bofors guns," Sharma said. "It's going to be stormy days in parliament."
On its part, the United Front says it is not worried about any threats to its survival.

"The government is absolutely confident," a senior United Front leader who asked not to be named told Reuters. "Congress is uncomfortable this government is surviving with their support. They are in no position to go to the polls."
